name: Omar Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Hartley and Shaw, a mid-size agency on the high street, and I mostly do lettings with a bit of sales. Day starts at half eight with the inbox, which is tenants chasing repairs and landlords chasing rent. Then I'm out doing viewings, maybe five or six, and check-ins where I walk a new tenant round with the inventory. I like the people side, the student who's nervous about their first flat. What wears me out is the landlords who treat a broken boiler as the tenant's problem.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you do it all from the inbox and the diary. How do you keep track of it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Paper diary, honestly, plus the office system because I have to. The others laugh at me, but I've never lost a key or missed a viewing in six years. Lena, my partner, is a nurse on shifts, so we plan our week on a calendar on the fridge. I don't use any of the AI writing tools the office pays for. I write my own listings, badly sometimes, but they're mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds like most of what the office talks about anyway. Lots of noise, a few shortcuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, to be honest. At the Friday drinks there's always someone saying the robots are coming for us, and I'd enjoy reminding them. Online I'd probably share something about how the real problem in housing was never software, it's rents and supply.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it means I keep my job and my way of working. The routine bits, like rent reminders and repair tickets, might get done by the system, and I'd be glad to lose those. My worry would still be the market, because when interest rates go up, sales dry up and the office gets tense about commission.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am, lettings mostly, and keep putting a third of my pay into savings like I have since I was twenty-two. I'd finally sit the lettings qualification the firm keeps offering, the one that gets me a pay step. And I'd keep pushing at the union branch for agents to get a proper base salary instead of living on commission.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. A bit smug, if I'm honest. The housing crisis would still make me angry, but that's not new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned commission. What happens to you in a slow year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In a slow year I drop maybe a fifth of my pay, because lettings fees are steady but the sales bonus disappears. I've got over a year's spending saved and a small flat my gran left me, which I rent out to a cousin cheaply. So a slow year stings, but it doesn't scare me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the office would you worry about, even in this calm picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jas on reception, because the system already books half the viewings online. If anything gets trimmed, it's the front desk first, not the people out doing viewings. Even in a boring year, the person answering the phone is the one the bosses look at.

say: I'd tell the Friday drinks crowd that **all the hype** about robots replacing agents came to nothing.
I'd post that the real housing problem is **rents and supply**, not software.
think: My **job and routine** stay mine, and losing rent reminders to software would be a small relief.
The **market cycle** is still the real threat, because commission dries up whenever interest rates rise.
do: Keep saving **a third** of my pay, as I have since I was twenty-two.
Sit the **lettings qualification** the firm offers to get the next pay step.
Push at the **union branch** for agents to get a proper base salary.
feel: **Relieved** and a little smug that the doom talk was wrong.
Still **angry** about the housing crisis, which has nothing to do with AI.
S0.quote: Even in a boring year, the person answering the phone is the one the bosses look at.
fieldNote: Omar is **secure**: over a year of savings and an inherited flat, so a slow year only stings.
His concern goes straight to **colleagues** at the front desk rather than himself.
Takes **pride** in doing things by hand, including writing his own listings and keeping a paper diary.
Frames everything through **housing politics**, not technology.

steps.text: Carry on with lettings and viewings at the same agency
Put a third of each month's pay into savings
Raise base salary for agents at the union branch meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That one's closer to what I already see creeping in at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say agents still matter, because nobody hands over the keys to their life savings to a chatbot. I'd also say firms shouldn't use it as an excuse to cut staff and keep the fees the same. That's the line I'd take at the union branch too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a good chunk of what I do is exactly that list: answering tenants, booking viewings, chasing references, writing listings. If software does all that, Hartley and Shaw needs fewer people like me per hundred properties. I'm average at the job, not a star, so I'm not sure I'm the one they'd keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd stop ignoring the office tools, as much as it annoys me, and get Jas or one of the younger lads to show me the basics. I'd move more of my time into check-ins, inventories and the awkward landlord conversations, the bits a program can't do. I'd also keep the savings untouched and stop the holiday we'd been planning to Portugal next spring, just to be safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I don't feel like I'm about to be sacked, but I feel like the floor's tilting a bit and I'm the one who refused to learn to walk on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd cancel Portugal. Is that about money or about nerves?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nerves, honestly. We could afford it ten times over with what's saved. But I'd want to feel I'd done something sensible, and not spending is the only sensible thing I know how to do without learning a new system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena about all this over dinner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Lena (my partner) that her job's safer than mine, which would make her laugh because she's always worried about the hospital cuts. Then I'd tell her I'll be fine, there are plenty of agencies round here. I'd half believe it.

say: I'd say **nobody hands over** their life savings to a chatbot, so agents still matter.
I'd argue firms must not use AI as **an excuse to cut** staff while keeping fees.
think: Much of my day is **answering, booking and chasing**, exactly the work software takes over.
I'm **average** at the job, so I doubt I'd be the one the agency keeps.
do: Ask a younger colleague to teach me **the office tools** in the first month.
Shift my time into **check-ins and inventories** that software can't do.
Cancel the **Portugal trip** next spring and leave savings untouched.
feel: **Uneasy**, as if the floor is tilting and he refused to learn to balance.
Not afraid of **the sack** yet, but less sure he'd be kept.
S1.quote: Nobody hands over the keys to their life savings to a chatbot.
fieldNote: Omar admits the scenario's task list matches **his own day** almost exactly.
His savings are large, so cutting the holiday is about **calming nerves**, not money.
Resistance to tech shows: learning the tools is framed as a **grudging concession**.
Leans on **plenty of local agencies** as reassurance, but only half believes it.

steps.text: Get a younger colleague to show him the office AI tools
Cancel next spring's holiday to Portugal
Argue at the union branch against using AI to cut staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's not long at all. I've only just got the hang of this job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud about it, I think. I'd say the government needs to stop it, or at least make firms keep people on and share the savings. I'd be at the union meetings and posting about it, which I've never really done before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job goes. If a machine can value a flat, write the listing, vet the tenant and talk a landlord down on fees, then the agency is just a website and a key box. The viewings could be done with a smart lock and a video tour. Robots don't even come into it for an agent, that's the scary bit, my work is mostly talking and paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd sit down with Lena and work out how long we last on savings plus the rent from my gran's flat, probably two years. I'd look at jobs where you have to be physically there, like housing officer for the council or a tenancy support role, where you visit people in trouble. I'd join every campaign going for a guaranteed income, and I'd stop putting money into anything risky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, properly. I'd be lying awake. It's the speed of it, there's no time to retrain into anything that isn't also going to get eaten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said agents are mostly talking and paperwork. Is there any hands-on part that buys you time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The check-ins, checking for damp, meter readings, walking people round. Maybe that gives me those three extra years before the robots. But that's a tiny slice of the job, and nobody pays an agent's wage for meter readings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger cousin, who rents your flat and is still at college?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my cousin to pick a course where you have to touch people or things, like nursing or plumbing, not marketing like he's doing now. And I'd tell him the rent stays the same as long as I've got the flat. That's about all I could promise.

say: I'd demand that **government** makes firms keep staff on and share the savings.
I'd turn up to **union meetings** and post online, which I've never done before.
think: My job **probably goes**, because AI can value, list, vet and negotiate.
An agency becomes **a website** and a key box, and robots aren't even needed.
do: Work out with Lena how long **savings and rent** last, roughly two years.
Apply for **council housing officer** or tenancy support roles that need home visits.
Join every campaign for a **guaranteed income** and stop risky spending.
feel: **Scared** and lying awake at night over how fast it moves.
**Trapped**, because any retraining target might be swallowed too.
S2.quote: Robots don't even come into it for an agent, that's the scary bit, my work is mostly talking and paperwork.
fieldNote: Omar sees his job as **mostly thinking work**, so the robot delay barely helps him.
Savings buy him **about two years**, which matters but doesn't calm him.
Turns to **collective and political action** for the first time in his life.
Aims for **face-to-face public roles**, which matches his progressive values.

steps.text: Apply for council housing officer and tenancy support jobs
Go to every union meeting about AI job cuts
Campaign online for a guaranteed basic income
Stop all big spending and hold savings in cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. That's a bit more breathing room than the last one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message as before but calmer, I think. I'd say we have five years, so use them: train people, protect renters, make the firms pay in. I'd want the union pushing for retraining money now, not after the fact.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still think agenting is finished by 2031, just not tomorrow. Five years is enough for me to get a different qualification while still earning. I'm twenty-seven, so I'd be thirty-two when it lands, which is young enough to start again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sign up for a part-time housing management course, the evening one at the college, which takes about two years. I'd keep doing lettings in the day and save harder, maybe half my pay since Lena and I don't have kids. I'd talk to the council about their tenancy officer jobs, which involve visiting homes and dealing with people in crisis. And I'd still go to the union meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but there's a plan in it. I can see a road from here to there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said save half your pay. What does that look like in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No new car, the old one does. Takeaways down to once a week. We'd probably stay in our rented place rather than buy, because I wouldn't want a big mortgage on a job that's ending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't like new tech. Would you use AI tools at work in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to, wouldn't I. Every agency will make you. I'd do the minimum and put my energy into the course, because learning a program I'll lose my job to feels like digging my own hole.

say: I'd say we have **five years**, so train people and protect renters now.
I'd want the union to push for **retraining money** before the cuts, not after.
think: **Agenting ends** by 2031, but five years lets me requalify while still earning.
At **thirty-two** I'd be young enough to start a new career.
do: Enrol in a **housing management course** at the college, about two years part time.
Save **half my pay** and skip buying a home or a new car.
Ask the council about **tenancy officer** jobs that involve visiting homes.
feel: **Worried** about the end of agenting, but steadier with a plan.
Some **hope**, because he can see a path from here.
S3.quote: Learning a program I'll lose my job to feels like digging my own hole.
fieldNote: The **extra three years** turn Omar's panic into a concrete course plan.
He would use AI only **grudgingly**, putting effort into leaving instead.
Decides **not to buy** a home, a real life choice driven by the scenario.
Still expects to **lose the job**, so anxiety stays even with savings.

steps.text: Enrol in the evening housing management course at the college
Save half of each month's pay
Apply for council tenancy officer jobs within two years
Put off buying a home and keep renting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That feels like forever and like nothing at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to fix it properly: retraining, rules on what firms can automate, and a decent safety net. Ten years is enough for governments to get it right if they bother. I'd be pushing that line at the union and with friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, ten years is a lot. I'd be thirty-seven, and I'd have had time to move into housing work or something else face to face. The bit that bothers me is that people always waste the warning time, and then it hits anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably do another year or two of lettings, get the qualification, then do the housing management course around year three. I'd keep saving a third of my pay, not half. Lena and I would likely still buy a small place, maybe in three or four years, once I'm in the new job. I'd keep up the union stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than scared. Ten years feels like seeing a storm out at sea, where you know it's coming but you can get the washing in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people waste warning time. Would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a bit, yes. I'm the sort to wait until the last minute, look at my diary. If I'm honest, years one to three I'd tell myself it's ages away and just carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you actually start early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing someone I know lose their job to it. If Jas on reception was let go and replaced by a chatbot, that would get me to the college the next week. I need it in front of me.

say: I'd say ten years is **enough time** to fix retraining and the safety net properly.
I'd push for **rules** on what firms can automate through the union.
think: At **thirty-seven** I'd have moved into housing work or another face-to-face job.
My worry is that people **waste the warning** time and it hits anyway.
do: Work **two more years** of lettings and finish the lettings qualification.
Start the **housing management course** around year three.
Keep saving **a third** of my pay and buy a small flat later.
feel: **Uneasy**, like watching a storm far out at sea.
Admits he'd **put off** acting until he sees someone lose their job.
S4.quote: Ten years feels like seeing a storm out at sea, where you know it's coming but you can get the washing in.
fieldNote: With a decade, Omar's mood drops to **uneasy**; age and savings carry him.
He openly admits he'd **procrastinate** for the first three years.
A **colleague's job loss** would be his real trigger to act.
Home-buying plans **return**, unlike in the five-year picture.

steps.text: Carry on with lettings for two more years before deciding
Start the housing management course around year three
Keep pushing the union for limits on automation

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. There's no time to move into something else before it eats that too. What would help is the council and housing charities hiring people like me to visit tenants, and a guaranteed income while we retrain, paid for by the firms that save the money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the tenants. If an agency becomes a website, who does a seventy-year-old renter ring when the boiler breaks at night? I worry about them more than me, because I've got savings and they've got nobody.

headlineQuote: If an agency becomes a website, who does a seventy-year-old renter ring when the boiler breaks at night?
portrait: Omar is a **27-year-old lettings agent** at a high-street agency, living with his partner Lena, a nurse.
He has **over a year's savings** and a flat inherited from his gran, so money isn't his main fear.
He **refuses AI tools**, keeps a paper diary and writes his own listings.
His mood rises from **calm** with a plateau to **alarmed** if AGI comes in two years.
He'd move toward **council housing work** and union campaigns, and worries most about vulnerable tenants.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to move into work that won't also be swallowed.
whatWouldHelp: **Council and charity jobs** visiting tenants, for people with agents' skills.
A **guaranteed income** during retraining, paid for by firms that save from automation.
